title: Network shapes and parameter counts
description: Map scalar connections to matrices using the shared network for Lessons16-20.
source_short: Backpropagation handout / PDF p.1; Assignment 1 / pp.1-3 / study parameters
source: Backpropagation_Derivation.pdf page 1; Assignment 1.pdf pages 1-3; numerical-practice.md N3.4 chosen parameters.

pages.title: One network for the next five lessons
pages.subtitle: Architecture and notation follow the backpropagation handout; numbers are study choices.
blocks: Input layer 0 has two features. Hidden layers 1 and 2 each have two sigmoid neurons. Layer 3 has one sigmoid output neuron.
Lessons 16-20 reuse the original N3.4 numerical-practice parameters. This lesson checks connections, shapes and counts before the full forward pass.

pages.title: Read the weight indices as an arrow
pages.subtitle: The handout writes the source index first and the destination index second.

blocks.eq: w_{i,j}^{(l)}:\quad\mathrm{source}\ i\ \mathrm{in\ layer}\ l-1\ \longrightarrow\ \mathrm{destination}\ j\ \mathrm{in\ layer}\ l

blocks: The bias is the weight from constant input 1. We store it separately as b. Do not also add a second constant-input bias if it is already included in b.
z is the weighted sum before activation; y is the activation after sigmoid. Known target labels will be written t.

pages.title: Count every weight and every bias
pages.subtitle: Each destination neuron has one weight per source neuron and one bias.
blocks: Input values are data, not trainable parameters. The sigmoid function adds no trainable parameter in this network.

pages.title: Record all original parameter values
pages.subtitle: Reset to this table whenever a later exercise says original parameters.
blocks: Layer 3 has only destination 1. Dashes mean those destination-2 connections do not exist; they are not additional zero-valued parameters.
These are chosen teaching values from numerical-practice.md, not numerical values supplied by the handout. The architecture and indexing come from the handout.

pages.title: Arrange connection weights into a matrix
pages.subtitle: Rows are sources; columns are destinations. The convention determines the multiplication.
blocks: Column 1 contains the two weights feeding hidden neuron 1. Column 2 contains the two weights feeding hidden neuron 2.

pages.title: Matrix multiplication is a list of dot products
pages.subtitle: For a single example, place input values in one row.
blocks: Each output entry pairs the input row with one destination column of W. The bias for that destination is added exactly once.

pages.title: Apply sigmoid to each entry separately
pages.subtitle: Activation changes the values, not the array shape.
blocks: This is elementwise activation, not a matrix inverse or a sigmoid of the sum of both entries. Lesson17 continues through the other two layers.

pages.title: Add a second example as another row
pages.subtitle: Use the same weights and biases for both examples.
blocks: Input X and output Z1 now both have shape 2 by 2. Each row keeps its own example; columns keep neuron identities.
Bias broadcasting means reuse [0,0.1] on each row. It does not create new learned biases for example B.

pages.title: Check dimensions before multiplying
pages.subtitle: Inner dimensions must agree; the outer dimensions give the result shape.
blocks: N counts examples; d(l) is the number of neurons in layer l, with d(0) equal to input features.
N = 2 here counts examples. The final 2 by 1 array has one prediction per example. Increasing N changes activation shapes, not the 15-parameter count.

pages.title: Your turn: a different small architecture
pages.subtitle: Use the same row-example and source-to-destination convention.
blocks: 1. Count all connection weights, all biases and total trainable parameters.
2. For a batch of four examples, give the shapes of X, W1, b1, Z1, W2, b2 and Z2.
3. For one input x = (1,0,-1), W1 has rows (1,2), (3,4), (5,6); b1 = (0.5,-0.5). Compute both entries of z1 by scalar multiplication.
Do not apply an activation in question 3: it asks for preactivation z.

pages.title: Practice answer: count and check shapes
pages.subtitle: A larger input width adds connections into every first-layer neuron.
blocks: Four examples share the same 11 parameters. Biases are broadcast over four rows, not trained separately for each row.

pages.title: Practice answer: multiply one row by columns
pages.subtitle: The zero input still has associated weights, even though its contribution is zero here.
blocks: Column 1 was (1,3,5); column 2 was (2,4,6). Multiplying by rows instead would mix up source and destination indices.
Checklist: identify rows and columns, check inner dimensions, add each bias once, and keep parameter count separate from batch size.
